**Plan created for question q_001: "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"**

A 9-item research plan (pl_002) was written to research.json. Here's what it covers:

---

### Background
So far, the only evidence placing Patrick Flynn as Thomas Flynn's son is the 1850 Schuylkill County census co-enumeration — an indirect/inferred connection, rated "possible" in the existing proof summary. The plan addresses that gap systematically.

---

### Plan Items (in execution order)

| # | Record Type | Place / Date | Repository | Why |
|---|-------------|--------------|------------|-----|
| pli_004 | 1860 Census | Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch | Patrick (~15) likely still in Thomas's household; a second decade of co-enumeration |
| pli_005 | 1870 Census | Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch | Patrick (~25); Thomas may appear in his household or vice versa |
| **pli_006** | **1870 Census** | **Schuylkill Co., PA** | **Ancestry** *(requested)* | Independent index — catches mis-transcriptions FamilySearch may miss |
| pli_007 | 1880 Census | Schuylkill Co., PA | FamilySearch | First federal census with explicit relationship to head; "father" stated would upgrade evidence |
| pli_008 | Church (baptism) | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1843–1847 | FamilySearch | Patrick's baptism would directly name both parents |
| pli_009 | Church (parents' marriage) | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1830–1848 | FamilySearch | Names Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother), confirms the couple |
| pli_010 | Probate (Thomas Flynn) | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1850–1910 | FamilySearch (image browse) | A will naming Patrick as son = direct parentage evidence |
| pli_011 | Death certificate (Patrick) | Pennsylvania, 1908 | PA State Archives | May name his parents and their birthplaces (secondary parentage evidence) |
| pli_012 | Land / FAN (Thomas Flynn) | Schuylkill Co., PA, 1840–1870 | County Recorder of Deeds | Deed witnesses/neighbors reveal kin network and may identify Patrick's mother's family |

---

### Next Steps
- **FamilySearch items** (pli_004, pli_005, pli_007, pli_008, pli_009, pli_010) → use **search-records**
- **Ancestry 1870 item** (pli_006) → use **search-external-sites**
- **PA State Archives & county courthouse** (pli_011, pli_012) → physical-access, contact repositories directly

openQuestions.question: Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?

questionStatuses.nextStep: proof-conclusion — concluded while blocked: re-conclude ps_001
proof-conclusion — resolved with no proof summary

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.exhaustive_search_summary: Only the 1850 census (FamilySearch, Ancestry, MyHeritage) has been searched for q_001. Post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records have not yet been searched.
items.narrative_markdown: Patrick Flynn appears in the 1850 census in Thomas Flynn's Schuylkill County household. Co-enumeration is indirect evidence that supports but does not prove parentage. Post-1860 censuses, probate, and church records have not yet been searched.

items.informant: Unknown household member (likely Thomas Flynn himself) reporting to census enumerator
items.informant_bias_notes: Census enumerator is the recorder, not the informant. As head of household, Thomas likely provided his own name, but the 1850 census does not identify the informant.

items.rationale: 1850 census fully indexed on FamilySearch. Free access, start here.
Ancestry has independent indexing; cross-check for transcription errors.
Third independent index for coverage confirmation.

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845) would be approximately 15 in 1860 and is likely still living in Thomas Flynn's household. The United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181) is name-searchable. A second decade of co-enumeration with Thomas Flynn would add an indirect data point extending the 1850 co-residence; the 1860 census does not explicitly record relationships, but continued household co-residence with Thomas strengthens the inferred parentage. Search Flynn, Flinn, and Flin variants. Free, name-searchable, and the highest-probability next source.

Patrick Flynn (~25 in 1870) may have established his own household or may still appear with Thomas Flynn. The United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Like 1860, the 1870 census does not record relationships, but continued co-enumeration or the appearance of Thomas Flynn in Patrick's own household across three decades materially supports the inferred parentage. Search Flynn, Flinn, and Flin variants. Free before paid.

Ancestry's independent index of the 1870 federal census (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7163/) uses a separate transcription and may surface entries missed or mis-transcribed in the FamilySearch index. Included per caller request as a cross-check for the same year. Name-searchable on Ancestry; search Flynn, Flinn, and Flin variants.

The 1880 census is the first federal census to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. Patrick Flynn (~35 in 1880) may appear as head of his own household with Thomas Flynn listed as 'father'; Thomas (if still alive, approximately 60-70) may appear in Patrick's household. The United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable. A 'son' or 'father' designation in 1880 would upgrade the parentage evidence from indirect co-enumeration (1850-1870) to a reported relationship, though still secondary information provided by the household head.

Patrick Flynn's baptism record (b. ~1845) would directly name both parents — the most direct parentage evidence available before civil registration. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985) is name-searchable; Roman Catholic and Protestant congregations in the anthracite coal region began keeping sacramental registers well before 1845. loc_001 notes some coal-region films are browse-only image groups, but SYNTH-PA-CHURCH reports a name-searchable index. Search Flynn, Flinn, and Flin variants in the 1843-1847 window.

A dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother is required for a parentage plan. The couple's marriage record: (a) confirms Thomas and the mother as a married couple; (b) supplies the mother's maiden name, which the 1850 census omits; and (c) by its date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth, corroborates Thomas as the father rather than merely a household head of the same surname. The Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable and covers the likely marriage window (roughly 1830-1848, dating back approximately 15 years before Patrick's birth). The date window is bounded by Thomas Flynn's plausible marriage age, not Patrick's own research window. Note the limit: the couple's marriage does not itself place Patrick as their child; a baptism or household record is still needed for that link.

Thomas Flynn was the head of household in the 1850 census, placing his birth approximately 1810-1830; he could plausibly have died anywhere between 1860 and 1910. The Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0) — this is an image browse of the county's probate dockets, not a name search. A will or letters of administration naming Patrick Flynn as a son would be direct evidence of parentage. loc_001 confirms probate records are held by the Schuylkill County Register of Wills, available from 1811. The date window is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research window.

Patrick Flynn died in 1908, after Pennsylvania's statewide civil death registration began in 1906 (per loc_001 quirks). A state death certificate should exist and may name his parents and their birthplaces. Death certificates are secondary evidence for parentage (the informant may not have known the parents accurately), but the 1908 certificate is the first primary-source record of death and a direct lead to parents' names. Pennsylvania death certificates from 1906 onward are held at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg.

For a parentage question at least one FAN item is required. Thomas Flynn's land transactions in the Schuylkill County grantee-grantor index name witnesses to deeds and — in each deed's boundary recital — the adjoining landowners, who are neighbors by definition and frequently relatives. These names form a FAN cluster around Thomas Flynn that may identify his wife's family surname, corroborate the mother's maiden name, or point to relatives who appear in Patrick Flynn's own records. This item targets what the land records reveal about Thomas Flynn's community and kin network, not any land fact about Patrick himself.

This plan is for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. **Mode: create — q_001: "Which probate or estate record names Caroline Voss's father?"**

**Survey of facts already recorded:**
- F1: Birth 1839, Rowan County, NC (unsourced)
- F2: Marriage ~1858, Rowan County, NC — sourced to S1 (Rowan County marriage record); a_002 explicitly notes no parents' names appear on that record
- No parents, no spouse, no other tree persons

---

**Plan pl_001 — 6 items:**

| ID | Record type | Place | Date window | Repository | Notes |
|----|-------------|-------|-------------|------------|-------|
| pli_001 | Probate | Rowan County, NC | 1839–1899 | FamilySearch | Collection 4000201; full-text keyword search for "Voss"/"Voas" preferred (index only ~40% complete); window sized to father's plausible lifespan |
| pli_002 | Census | Rowan County, NC | 1850 | FamilySearch | Caroline ~11 in 1850, almost certainly in father's household; establishes father's given name and birth year |
| pli_003 | Census | Rowan County, NC | 1860 | FamilySearch | Collection 1473181; fallback for pli_002; father's household; also reveals siblings as FAN leads |
| pli_004 | Vital record (parents' marriage) | Rowan County, NC | 1820–1842 | FamilySearch | Collection 4000202; Voss groom in this window is the candidate father; supplies mother's maiden name |
| pli_005 | Vital record (FAN — sibling marriages) | Rowan County, NC | 1855–1885 | FamilySearch | Same collection 4000202; sibling marriages may name the father directly or show him as witness |
| pli_006 | Probate | Rowan County, NC | 1839–1899 | Ancestry | Fallback for pli_001; Ancestry's Rowan County holdings may cover estate abstracts not yet on FamilySearch |

---

**Rationale:**

The plan targets the father's probate estate first, since the research question explicitly asks for the probate or estate record that names Caroline Voss's father. He was likely born around 1800–1820 and died sometime before 1900, so the 1839–1899 window covers his plausible adult and later years. Because FamilySearch's Rowan County probate index is only about 40% complete, a full-text keyword search on "Voss"/"Voas" is preferred over a strict name search.

If probate alone does not identify the father by given name, the 1850 and 1860 census searches will locate the Voss household and establish the father's given name for a more targeted follow-up. The parents' marriage record search would supply both the father's and mother's names and corroborate parentage by date. Sibling marriage records are included as FAN leads — a sibling's marriage may name the same father independently. Ancestry is held in reserve if FamilySearch probate comes up empty.

---

**Next steps:** Run **search-records** for pli_001–pli_005 (FamilySearch), starting with the Rowan County probate full-text search for "Voss" across 1839–1899, then the 1850 census. Use **search-external-sites** for pli_006 (Ancestry) if the FamilySearch probate search is unproductive.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

- Parent I3: Unknown Sheahan — no facts, gender unknown
- Hypothesis h_001 is active: move was for anthracite coal employment; no supporting or contradicting assertions yet

**pl_001 — items in execution order:**

- **pli_001** — census, Schuylkill County / national, FamilySearch, 1880 — Collection 1417683 (United States Census, 1880), name-searchable; fills the critical 1870–1882 gap and places Michael geographically and occupationally at the midpoint; search Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan, Shahan variants
- **pli_002** — census (FAN), Schuylkill County / national, FamilySearch, 1880 — same collection 1417683, name-searchable; targets Patrick Sheahan (I2, brother), who purchased Schuylkill County property in 1875 — seven years before Michael's known arrival — to test whether Michael followed an established family chain-migration network into the coalfields
- **pli_003** — census, Schuylkill County / national, FamilySearch, 1900 — Collection 1325221 (United States Census, 1900), name-searchable; uniquely captures years of immigration, months married, and years in state, narrowing Michael's pre-Schuylkill origin or immigration year to frame the naturalization browse below
- **pli_004** — church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, 1878–1892 — Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable; Catholic parish register would show when Michael affiliated with a Schuylkill County parish and may name the prior parish of origin; locality guide notes these parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia through 1961
- **pli_005** — land, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, 1875–1892 — Image group 007936752 (Deed Records, 1815–1900), browse-only; coal-region land was frequently leased not purchased, so Michael may not appear, but Patrick's post-1875 transactions and any Michael entry would show economic anchoring for the move; browse the Sheahan/Sheehan name range
- **pli_006** — immigration/naturalization, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, 1860–1895 — Image group 007936750 (Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images), browse-only; declarations would state country and often parish of origin, first US residence, and arrival date — direct evidence of the migration path before Schuylkill County; browsed after item 3 whose immigration-year field can focus the decade

**Fallback relationships:** No fallback chains in this plan; each item targets a distinct record type or period. Items 5 and 6 are browse-only and are sequenced after their indexed counterparts (items 1–4) have narrowed the scope.

**Total scope:** 7 searches — 4 name-searchable, 2 browse-only image reviews, 1 written inquiry to a historical society.

---

The second search looks at his brother Patrick in the same census, since Patrick bought property in Schuylkill County in 1875 — seven years before Michael arrived — and following a family member into an established mining community was one of the most common reasons an Irish-American laborer changed county and occupation. After that, the plan moves to the 1900 census (which records years of immigration and years in the state), then Catholic parish records, then deed records and naturalization papers held as browse-only image films, and finally a written inquiry to the Schuylkill County Historical Society.

**Next step:** Run the two 1880 census searches on FamilySearch — looking for Michael Sheahan (and variants Sheehan, Shehan, Shahan) via pli_001, and for Patrick Sheahan via pli_002. Hand those to **search-records** when ready.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

items.claim: Michael Sheahan relocated to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania between 1870 and 1882 for anthracite coal-mining employment
items.notes: Supported only by the occupation/location change visible across log_001 (1870, farmer, elsewhere) and log_002 (1882, miner, Schuylkill County). No direct record of the move's cause -- no land transaction, employment record, letter, or newspaper item -- has been found for Michael himself yet.

entry.rationale: The 1880 U.S. Federal Census is the only indexed record known to fall inside the 1870–1882 gap (log_001 established the 1870 'before' point; log_002 established the 1882 'after' point). Finding Michael in Schuylkill County in 1880 as a miner would show the move predates the 1882 directory entry; finding him elsewhere as a farmer would compress the move window to 1880–1882. Collection 1417683 ('United States Census, 1880') is name-searchable. Search surname variants Sheehan, Shehan, and Shahan alongside Sheahan.

FAN item targeting Patrick Sheahan (I2, Michael's brother). The tree records Patrick buying property in Schuylkill County in 1875 (Deed Book 42, p. 118, source S2) — seven years before Michael's known 1882 arrival. A well-established sibling in the coal region is a documented pull factor for chain migration; confirming Patrick's 1880 household, occupation, and employer in Schuylkill County would test whether Michael followed family into an existing mining network rather than arriving independently for wage reasons. Searched in the same collection (1417683, name-searchable) as item 1. Search surname variants as above.

Collection 1325221 ('United States Census, 1900') is name-searchable and uniquely captures years of immigration, months married, and years in the state — fields absent from the 1880 census and the 1882 directory. If Michael was foreign-born, the immigration year would date his first US arrival and show whether he came directly to Pennsylvania or migrated internally; if US-born, the state-of-birth column narrows the pre-Schuylkill jurisdiction and frames further searches. Either outcome sharpens the motivation analysis. Search with surname variants.

Collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH ('Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records') is name-searchable (personCount 982,415), covering 1708–1985. If Michael was Roman Catholic — the dominant faith among Irish coal-region migrants — a parish register entry for his arrival, baptism transfer, or sacrament (marriage, confirmation) would establish when he affiliated with a Schuylkill County parish and might name his prior parish of origin. The locality guide (loc_001) notes that Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) through 1961, and that sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese, not the county. The FamilySearch indexed collection covers digitized parish records from the county. Search surname variants.

Image group 007936752 (Deed Records, 1815–1900, 543 images) is browse-only (personCount 0). The locality guide (loc_001) notes that coal-region land was often leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers, so a deed for Michael may not exist; however, even a lease or deed in Patrick's name after 1875 (Deed Book 42, p. 118, already in the tree as S2) could show whether Michael's arrival coincided with a property transaction — a tangible economic anchor for the move. Browse the volume for entries in the surname range Sheahan/Sheehan in the 1878–1890 span.

Image group 007936750 (Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images) is browse-only (personCount 0). The locality guide (loc_001) flags these as browse-only image groups requiring page-by-page review. If Michael or Patrick were Irish-born, their naturalization declarations would state the country and, frequently, the county or parish of origin, along with first US residence and date of arrival — direct evidence of the migration path that precedes Schuylkill County. Browsed after the 1900 census (item 3), whose immigration-year field can focus the decade to check.

County and anthracite-region histories, including biographical sketch volumes published in the late nineteenth century, sometimes document when early mine workers arrived, where they came from, and what occupation they held before entering the coalfields. These are derivative records but provide leads to original evidence explaining the move's motivation — the question hypothesis h_001 ('moved for anthracite coal employment') will remain untested by census and church records alone if no employment record is found. The Schuylkill County Historical Society (Pottsville, Pennsylvania) holds local histories and county periodicals not available online. This item is last because access requires written or in-person inquiry and the probability of a named entry for Michael Sheahan is lower than for the indexed sources above.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

If his occupation was something other than mining, that would show he took up mining on arriving in Schuylkill. Variant spellings: Sheahan, Sheehan, Shehan.

Because the film is browse-only, pages must be examined image by image. The 1880 census result (item 1) will confirm whether foreign birth is indicated, sharpening this item's priority.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

---

**What we know about Martha J:**
- Born ~1859 in Georgia (no source; recorded as tree fact)
- Used surname **"Wood"** when she married W. F. Lanham in Smith County, TX, 7 Jan 1869
- Later married James M. Neal in Hill County, TX, 31 Jul 1879 as "Mattie Landham" (a widow's styling from her Lanham marriage)
- **No parents recorded** anywhere in the tree or assertions

**Note:** "Wood" *may* be a prior married name rather than her birth surname — this will be tested in the plan.

**The 8 Plan Items (in execution order):**

| # | What | Where | Why |
|---|------|--------|-----|
| pli_001 | 1860 Census | Blount County, Alabama | An unverified prior tree source links Martha to an "M M Wood" household here; would directly reveal parents |
| pli_002 | 1860 Census | Georgia statewide | Martha's recorded birthplace; as an infant she'd be in her parents' household |
| pli_003 | Marriage records | Smith County, TX, 1857–1868 | Tests whether "Wood" is a prior married name before her Lanham marriage |
| pli_004 | Marriage records | Blount County, Alabama, 1840–1870 | Searching for the *parents'* marriage — would give the mother's maiden name |
| pli_005 | Marriage records | Georgia statewide, 1840–1865 | Fallback if the family was in Georgia instead of Alabama |
| pli_006 | Probate records | Blount County, Alabama, 1870–1920 | A parent's will naming Martha as heir would be direct parentage evidence |

| pli_008 | 1870 Census (FAN) | Smith County, Texas | Places Martha in the Lanham household; neighboring Wood relatives may reveal the county of origin |

Once a county of origin is confirmed, a Georgia locality survey should be requested to add any county-level records (church, land, court) that may further corroborate parentage.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Thomas Flynn (born ~1818) would be approximately 52 and Patrick Flynn (born ~1845) approximately 25. Searching both names fills the high-severity timeline gap identified for 1860-1908. Thomas's 1870 household would reveal any remaining children still at home, adding to the chain of indirect evidence established by the 1850 and 1860 censuses. Though the 1870 census lacks a relationship column, continued co-residence with Thomas would extend the household-position evidence. Variant spellings Flyn and Flinn should be checked.

United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable and is the most important remaining census for this question: the 1880 schedule was the first federal census to include a relationship-to-head-of-household column. If Thomas Flynn (~62) still heads a household, any co-resident children would be explicitly designated 'Son' or 'Daughter,' converting the indirect household-position evidence of 1850 and 1860 into a direct relationship statement. Patrick Flynn (~35) likely heads his own household by 1880; finding his entry would also place him in the county for the intervening decades. Variant spellings Flyn and Flinn should be checked.

Ancestry independently transcribed the 1880 census from the same NARA microfilm and may have captured variant spellings or resolved transcription differences that the FamilySearch index missed. The underlying record is identical, so any Thomas Flynn household found here carries the same evidentiary weight — the explicit relationship column applies equally. Searched as fallback if pli_007 (FamilySearch 1880) yields no useful result.

United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable. Patrick Flynn (~55) would appear in his own household in Schuylkill County. The 1900 schedule records the number of children born and surviving for each married woman and includes a relationship column, which would characterize Patrick's family structure. Patrick is confirmed dead by 1908 (death cert), so 1900 is the last census likely to show him alive. Searching this year closes the final census gap in the subject's timeline. Variant spellings Flyn and Flinn should be checked.

Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0); Schuylkill County probate volume 007936749 (1851-1930) is also browse-only (personCount 0). The loc_001 locality entry confirms the Schuylkill County Register of Wills has held probate records since 1811. Thomas Flynn was born ~1818 (project tree) and was alive in 1860; this item's date range (1861-1900) is set by his estimated lifespan — a parent born ~1818 could plausibly survive into his early 80s. A will naming Patrick as 'my son' would be direct evidence of parentage, stronger than any inference drawn from census household position. An administration bond or estate inventory naming Patrick as an heir would carry similar weight. The proof summary ps_001 explicitly identifies Thomas Flynn's probate as a primary remaining gap.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415, covering 1708-1985). This item targets two records: (1) Thomas Flynn and his wife's marriage — a dedicated parents'-marriage item is required for this parentage question; Thomas married before Patrick's birth in ~1845, so search approximately 1835-1848; the couple's marriage record confirms Thomas and his wife as a unit and supplies the mother's maiden name, which census and death records have not provided; by its date relative to Patrick's birth it also corroborates the parentage inference drawn from census co-residence alone. (2) Thomas Flynn's church burial — PA statewide civil death registration did not begin until 1906 (loc_001 quirk), so if Thomas died before 1906 his burial register is the record to find; a burial entry sometimes names surviving children, further corroborating the family unit and bounding the probate search window. The date range spans both the marriage window and the plausible burial window for Thomas.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. Search for Patrick Flynn's marriage record. The death certificate informant was James Brown, Patrick's son-in-law, so Patrick had at least one married daughter, placing his marriage approximately 1865-1895. Catholic marriage records in Pennsylvania sometimes stated the groom's parents and birthplace. An independent statement of Patrick's parents in his own marriage record would provide evidence of parentage distinct from census co-residence and the secondary-informant death certificate.

Volume 007936753 (Schuylkill County Marriage Records, 1870-1910) is browse-only (personCount 0). If the indexed church collection (pli_012) does not return Patrick Flynn's marriage, this volume of civil marriage registers covers the same period and must be examined page by page. The marriage record could name Patrick's parents or birthplace. Searched as fallback for pli_012.

Volume 007936752 (Schuylkill County Deed Records, 1815-1900) is partially searchable (22% record-searchable per volume_search). FAN item — required for a parentage question. Deeds in which Thomas Flynn and Patrick Flynn both appear as grantor, grantee, or as adjacent landowners named in boundary recitals (per Appendix B: boundary recitals routinely name adjoining landowners who are often kin) bear directly on the parentage relationship. A deed in which Thomas conveys land 'to my son Patrick' would be direct evidence. Even absent such a deed, witnesses and neighboring landowners named alongside Thomas and Patrick may identify other relatives who could corroborate the family connection. The 22% searchable portion can be name-searched; the remainder would require browsing.

Swedish Lutheran clergy maintained these detailed household registers from 1688 (church law of 1686 per loc_002); each household entry records where each member was born or previously resided. Locating Jöns Jönsson's household listing will show Elena's stated origin parish — the most direct Swedish record type for tracing a person's birthplace.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

This plan is for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were, given that a newly found reference suggests his father Thomas likely died around 1865 rather than later. The previous search window for Thomas's probate records (1870-1890) was built on the wrong assumption, so the plan now targets the 1860-1870 period instead. First, a search of Schuylkill County probate records in that corrected window will look for Thomas Flynn's will or estate administration, which could directly name Patrick as a son and give the project its strongest original-record proof of parentage. Second, a search of the 1870 census will check whether Thomas has disappeared from the records by that point (supporting the ca. 1865 death) and whether his widow appears as head of a household that includes Patrick or his siblings — which would also help identify Patrick's mother by name.

The next step is to search FamilySearch for the corrected Schuylkill County probate records in 1860-1870, then follow with the 1870 census check.
